title: Two chariots
hook: two gods meet on a narrow road; the unrighteous won't yield and falls (Jataka 457)

segments.voice: Yesterday, two otters' quarrel, one fish, and the jackal who judged between them. Your line was the judge ate the fish. Did you settle something fairly? Today, a narrow road, high in the air. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

Two chariots, nose to nose on a road with room for only one, and neither driver will back up. It could be any narrow lane on any weekday morning. In this Jataka tale the road runs through the sky, and the drivers are gods. One is named Dhamma, righteousness. The other is Adhamma, its opposite. Each has somewhere to be, and each expects the other to move. Today, two chariots.
screen: `A ROAD WITH ROOM FOR ONE.` → `TWO GODS, NOSE TO NOSE.` → `DHAMMA AND ADHAMMA.`

segments.voice: First, the meeting. In the tale, both gods travel through the world in their chariots, and one day their paths cross head on, in a place where only one can pass. Second, the claims. Each tells the other to get out of the way, and each makes his case. Adhamma's case is force: he is strong, and he does not give way to anyone. Dhamma's case is his goodness, and the honor the wise give it. Third, the refusal. Adhamma will not yield. Not an inch. He even offers to fight for the road. Dhamma's answer, in the tale's last verse between them, is that if Adhamma really is the stronger, he'll swallow the harsh words and make way for him. And at the very moment Dhamma says it, Adhamma topples from his chariot headfirst, and the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the road goes on. Dhamma, the Bodhisatta in this tale, continues on his way. The story doesn't have Dhamma win by shoving harder. He never rams the other chariot. The one who insists on never yielding is the one who falls, and the road opens for the one who was willing to give it up. Some readers find the whole point in that fall: what cannot bend at all eventually breaks. On an ordinary road, letting someone go first costs a few seconds. In a family argument it might cost a little pride. The tale suggests that refusing can cost a great deal more. So yielding here isn't weakness, and it isn't losing. It's how the road stays open.
screen: `TWO GODS, ONE NARROW ROAD.` · `EACH CLAIMS THE WAY.` · `ADHAMMA WILL NOT YIELD.` · `THE STUBBORN ONE FALLS.` · then, large: `YIELDING WINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, and find somewhere in the body that's braced. Shoulders, jaw, hands. That's the body refusing to give way. Breathe out, and let it yield a little. Then think of one place today where you'll meet someone head on: a doorway, a meeting, a merge on the road, a conversation that tends to dig in. Decide now to let them go first, once. The bell holds the time.
Two chariots. A Jataka tale: righteousness and its opposite meet on a narrow road, and the one who will not yield is the one who falls. Today's word.
Your line: yielding wins. Today, yield once, on purpose, and notice what it actually costs. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Dhamma, the Pali form of the Sanskrit dharma, is one of the Three Jewels Buddhists take refuge in, together with the Buddha and the Sangha.

fork.setup: you're Adhamma, nose to nose with Dhamma on a road with room for one, and neither of you will move. what do you do?
options: back up and let him pass.
fork.reveal: in the tale Adhamma refuses to yield. when Dhamma says he'll bear the harsh words and make way, Adhamma falls headfirst from his chariot.

original.note: Pali: dhamma, the teaching, what is right; in this tale it is also the name of the righteous god.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about road rage among gods.
what it means: the one who will not yield is the one who falls, and the road stays open for the other.
what a scholar hears: the names are a pair, dhamma and adhamma, righteousness and its negation, and in the tale Dhamma is the Bodhisatta.

notes: Jataka 457 paraphrased: Dhamma (the Bodhisatta) and Adhamma meet in chariots in the sky; each claims the road; Adhamma refuses to yield, falls headfirst and is swallowed by the earth; Dhamma goes on. Confirm the content of each god's claim and whether Dhamma offers to yield in the verses; the script avoids saying he does.
The carry 'yielding wins' is the index line; the teach reads it as 'the one who refuses to yield falls', which fits the outline hook.
Editor: removed a repeated 'Notice what the story doesn't do' turn (same device on days 822, 826 and through this week).

Audit: the teach had Adhamma fall 'at that very moment' of his own refusal; in the tale (Cowell vol. 4) he falls at the moment the Bodhisatta speaks his verse offering to bear the harsh words and make way. Teach and fork reveal now say so, which also makes the carry 'yielding wins' literal. Keeper to confirm the reading of that verse (some read it as defiant rather than forbearing).
